sections.label: Act I — The Perfect Trap
sections.text: CAD gives you exact numbers. Manufacturing gives you a range. A pin designed at ten millimeters might land slightly larger; the hole might land slightly smaller. Therefore, zero gap is a trap.
sections.speaker_directions: Keep the first two sentences symmetrical. Slow slightly through the pin-versus-hole contrast. Land hard on 'trap.'

delivery_cues.delivery_note: Make the range feel inevitable, then deliver the consequence.

sections.label: Act II — Tolerance Is Not Clearance
sections.text: That range is tolerance: how far the real part can drift from nominal. Clearance is different. It's the space you choose between mating surfaces, so their tolerance zones never collide.
sections.speaker_directions: Teach the two definitions with calm precision. Pause before 'Clearance is different' and brighten slightly as the idea becomes useful.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: This is the conceptual hinge; preserve contrast and intelligibility.

sections.label: Act II — Three Jobs, Three Fits
sections.text: Want movement? Choose a clearance fit. Want location with light force? A transition fit. Want a permanent grip? An interference fit. Same geometry—three completely different jobs.
sections.speaker_directions: Build a crisp three-beat rhythm. Each question is slightly quicker; slow and widen on the final summary.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: Let each fit feel like a distinct tool choice, not a vocabulary list.

enhancement_cues.description: Three-part mechanical triptych: slider moves freely, keyed pin seats with a click, press-fit pin locks under force.

sections.label: Act III — Test the Process
sections.text: But there is no magic gap for every printer, material, or process. Print a tiny fit gauge first: several pins, several gaps, one quick test. Then put the winning value into your design.
sections.speaker_directions: Reject the magic-number myth firmly, then become practical and encouraging. Accelerate gently through the three-part test list.
